To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified several iron transport systems in the gonococcus and that these proteins could be used as components of a vaccine to protect women against gonocococcal infections.

(1) the gonococcus uses the human host iron transport protein, transferrin, as an iron source; (2) transferrin is bound and transported by the gonococcus using a complex of proteins, the transferrin receptor, and a TonB-dependent outer membrane protein, TbpA; and (3) the gonococcal transferrin receptor complex is a potential vaccine antigen.
the transferrin- iron transport system is not phase variable and is expressed by most gonococci.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying and characterizing the gonococcal transferrin-binding protein complex and other iron acquisition systems.
the development of a vaccine for gonorrhea and other Neisseria infections.
the identification and characterization of potential vaccine antigens for the prevention and treatment of gonorrhea.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transferrin-transport system is a good candidate for vaccine formulation.
gonococcal vaccines will be developed in the near future.
the transferrin-transport system is an important candidate antigen for inclusion in a vaccine for gonococcal disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a number of potential vaccine candidates and have begun to characterize the immune responses that are generated by these antigens.
we have identified and characterized a number of iron transport proteins that are potential vaccine candidates.
the transferrin-transport system of the gonococci was shown to be a potential target for vaccine development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gonococcus is a complex pathogen with multiple iron transport systems.
the gonococcus can be manipulated genetically and the resulting mutants can be used to define the role of specific genes in pathogenesis.
transferrin-binding protein A (TbpA) and transferrin-binding-protein B (TbpB) are promising vaccine candidates against Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
